Here the latency requirement and the availability requirement point the same way, which makes the design simpler. A flag call over the network on every render is slow, and it is also a single point of failure: if the flag service is down, nothing renders. So keep the flag values next to the render code. Refresh them in the background from the flag service, delivered through a CDN (content delivery network — servers near the user that cache and serve files). Rendering never waits for a network round trip.

worst_places.quote: The fan-out bottleneck is architectural: a single server process holding all WebSocket connections for a popular document caps out — you need a pub-sub layer (Redis Pub/Sub, or a dedicated message broker) so any server instance handling a client's connection can publish a cursor update once, and every other instance subscribed to that document's channel relays it to its own connected clients, decoupling "how many users are viewing this document" from "how many connections one process can hold".

worst_places.before: The fan-out bottleneck is architectural: a single server process holding all WebSocket connections for a popular document caps out — you need a pub-sub layer (Redis Pub/Sub, or a dedicated message broker) so any server instance handling a client's connection can publish a cursor update once, and every other instance subscribed to that document's channel relays it to its own connected clients, decoupling "how many users are viewing this document" from "how many connections one process can hold".
worst_places.after: The fan-out bottleneck — sending one update out to many listeners — is architectural. One server process cannot hold all the WebSocket connections for a popular document; it hits its connection limit. The fix is a pub-sub layer: Redis Pub/Sub, or a dedicated message broker. Whichever server instance holds a client's connection publishes that client's cursor update once, to the document's channel. Every other instance subscribed to that channel relays the update to its own connected clients. This decouples "how many users are viewing this document" from "how many connections one process can hold".

worst_places.quote: For statistical rigor: fixed-horizon testing (waiting for a pre-computed sample size before looking) avoids the classic "peeking" error, but a Bayesian or sequential-testing approach with proper alpha-spending lets you check results early without inflating the false-positive rate — the trap is checking a p-value repeatedly as data comes in and stopping the moment it crosses 0.05, which invalidates the statistics entirely regardless of which framework you're nominally using.
worst_places.problem: system-design-q-23. Eight unfamiliar concepts stack up in one 68-word sentence with nothing to hold on to: fixed-horizon testing, pre-computed sample size, the peeking error, Bayesian approach, sequential testing, alpha-spending, false-positive rate, p-value and the 0.05 threshold. No example, no number, no analogy. "Alpha-spending" is never explained anywhere in the file. This is a frontend question bank — statistics is exactly where the target reader has no background to fall back on.
worst_places.before: For statistical rigor: fixed-horizon testing (waiting for a pre-computed sample size before looking) avoids the classic "peeking" error, but a Bayesian or sequential-testing approach with proper alpha-spending lets you check results early without inflating the false-positive rate — the trap is checking a p-value repeatedly as data comes in and stopping the moment it crosses 0.05, which invalidates the statistics entirely regardless of which framework you're nominally using.
worst_places.after: For statistical rigor, decide up front when you are allowed to look at the results. The trap is "peeking": you watch the p-value (the chance of seeing this result if the variants were really identical) as data comes in, and you stop the test the moment it drops below 0.05. Do that and you will find a "winner" in tests where both variants are identical, because you gave yourself many chances to hit 0.05 by luck. Two ways out. Fixed-horizon testing: compute the needed sample size before you start, and do not look until you reach it. Or sequential/Bayesian testing with alpha-spending: you may look early, but each early look costs part of your error budget, so the total false-positive rate stays where you set it. Either framework is invalidated by peeking, so the framework name alone protects nothing.

patterns: The `Senior nuance` dumping ground WAS inherited, just without the label. All 25 answers use one fixed shape: `### <thesis heading>` -> 1-3 prose paragraphs -> code -> one or two closing paragraphs that pack the three or four hardest facts of the topic into a single 45-78-word sentence -> `**Common pitfall:**`. In 16 of 25 EN answers the last prose paragraph before the pitfall is literally one sentence, and in 21 of 25 it is 40+ words. That paragraph is where nearly all of the 256 flagged over-long sentences live, and it is the one paragraph in each answer with no example, no code and no numbers. Fixing this one slot would move the flag density more than any other change.

The house sentence is `<framing clause>: <fact A>, so <fact B> — <fact C>, <fact D>` — a colon followed by an em-dash-chained tail. The punctuation already marks the seams, so almost every over-limit sentence can be split at its own existing colon and em-dashes into 3-4 sentences with zero content loss. This is a mechanical fix, not a rewrite.

The `### <thesis>` heading is a genuinely good pattern and is the main thing propping up Rubric C — every one of the 25 headings is a real claim, not a topic label. But the first body paragraph then restarts from zero instead of continuing the heading, usually with a negation or framing warm-up: `The naive model —`, `The naive answer —`, `The naive heuristic (...)`, `The part that makes this harder`, `The part that actually trips teams up`, `The whole point of X is`, `There are two separate problems here`, `At small scale, X wins`. Nine of 25 answers open this way, and in four of them (q-4, q-11, q-13, q-18) the specific thing the question asked for lands only after the code block.

The `[Article Name]` bracket-reference habit was NOT inherited: the bank contains zero plain-text bracket references. It also contains zero real links and zero diagrams — in the one topic where the site's diagram primitive would pay off most (fan-out via pub-sub in q-24, host/remote isolation in q-18, compliance-aware failover in q-22, the three-tier token hierarchy in q-15). Four or five diagrams would absorb the densest closing paragraphs directly.

RU is the shorter and plainer locale; EN is the harder one. EN is 11% longer (6952 vs 6251 words), has 14 more over-limit sentences, and carries all the idiom load. But RU pays for it in two other ways: English nouns inflected with an apostrophe (tree-shake'ить, remote'у, tombstone'ов, broadcast'ов) and untranslated English noun phrases sitting bare in Russian sentences (blast radius, sparse fieldsets, ingestion pipeline, happy-path, fire-and-forget, drop-oldest, комплаенс-регион).
notes: The `**Common pitfall:**` block is the best-written part of the bank — a concrete wrong choice plus its concrete consequence, present in all 25 answers — but it is itself a single 40-50-word em-dash sentence every time, so it inherits the same B defect. Code quality is otherwise high: self-contained, commented at the non-obvious lines, no cross-example state; the only real E defects are line width (~120 lines over 82 chars, RU worse than EN) and mislabelled fence languages. Bureaucratic RU markers are essentially absent (no «является», «осуществляется», «в случае если»); the RU problem is calque, not officialese. Question stems sometimes expand an abbreviation the answer then uses bare (BFF, CSP, SRI, ABAC), which is why those are not in the unexpanded list — but TTL, CDN, SSE, SSR, SSG, ORM, CI and DOM are expanded nowhere in either locale.
